Quand la communauté nourrit le quartier: When the Community Feeds the Neighbourhood

Le Frigo Communautaire de Saint-Henri et: The Frigo Communautaire de Saint-Henri and volunteer Cécile Lars. Photo: Christelle Saint-Julien
À Saint-Henri, le <l1>Frigo Communautair: In Saint-Henri, the <l1>Frigo Communautaire</l1> is a gathering point whose popularity would be the envy of any business. In an area many describe as a food desert, and where <l2>gentrification is gaining ground</l2>, residents are pitching in to help one another. For the past few weeks, the shared fridge has sat in its new location, in a custom-built wooden shelter. Throughout the day, visitors are greeted by the cheerful shouts of children from the neighbouring elementary school. “I think there’s a real need in Saint-Henri; there’s a lot of food insecurity,” says Cécile Lars, a volunteer with the community fridge.
Au Québec, ce sont 17 % des ménages qui: In Quebec, 17% of households live with food insecurity. “The community fridge is for everyone,” Ms. Lars insists. “It’s set up so that anyone, at any hour, can freely drop off or take food,” says the woman, who has lived in the neighbourhood for 10 years. Whether it’s families who need a helping hand, local kids stopping by for a snack, businesses leaving their unsold goods or residents with extra food, everyone uses it. For Ms. Lars, an initiative like this goes beyond judgments and stereotypes. “It’s not about being poor, destitute, in misery or on the street: it’s about food, and food should be shared and given.
Si on en a plus, il faut que ça finisse: If you have more than you need, it should end up in someone’s mouth,” she believes. One thing is certain: everything goes fast, with hundreds of people opening the door of the fridge and the adjoining pantry every week. “When the fridge is full, it’s empty within three hours. We don’t put in enough, we’d need more,” says Ms. Lars. Ahmed Chebbi first came across the fridge by chance, close to his home. He thought someone had left it there by mistake, and he was completely surprised when he opened the door. Mr. Chebbi, who has lived in the neighbourhood since 2018, is one of the people who get involved in the community fridge initiative. “Sometimes people can’t get there, so I take the food and bring it to them,” he explains, citing the difficulties neighbourhood residents have had feeding themselves because of COVID-19 and rising food prices.
Selon le Rapport sur les prix alimentair: According to Canada’s Food Price Report, Canadian households spent an average of $695 more on their grocery basket in 2021. This year, food prices have risen an average of 3.8%, the largest increase in 12 years, and researchers are predicting a further increase of 5 to 7% in 2022.
Il y a huit ans, alors en convalescence,: Eight years ago, while recovering from an illness, Darren Gerbrandt decided to act on his idea of a self-serve fridge. “I had the time, I had no more excuses. I’d wanted to set up a community fridge for a long time. I had already been involved in a similar project in Winnipeg in the 1990s,” he tells us over the phone. That’s how he launched the first initiative of its kind in Montréal, putting a fridge at everyone’s disposal in the yard of the building where he lives. “A month later, I was already making Christmas meals. And it keeps growing.
Aujourd’hui, il y a de plus en plus de f: Today, more and more fridges are appearing around the city.” Although he has passed the torch, he says he couldn’t be happier to see the project grow, some seven years later.
« Obtenir des ressources et trouver un e: “Getting resources and finding a location are the two hardest things about starting a project like this,” says the founder, who faced many organizational challenges. He remembers the happy moments. “A young man once told me: ‘Thank you so much, if it weren’t for you, I wouldn’t have had any yogurt today,’” he says, adding that he shed a tear after hearing that.
« Il y a eu un beau moment. Je marchais: “There was one great moment. I was walking down the street with my punk friends, and the police stopped to say thank you to me.”
« Avec ce genre d’entreprise, on a beauc: “With this kind of undertaking, you have a lot to deal with when it comes to ‘not in my backyard,’” explains Cécile Lars, standing firmly in front of the fridge, coffee in hand. While people are in favour of a project like this, they often don’t want it near their homes. Ms. Lars explains that because the fridge is meant for everyone, its clientele displeases many. The Saint-Henri fridge has had several locations before ending up in the alley, hooked up to the home of one of the volunteers. It needs electricity, but also “the agreement and enthusiastic participation of people,” as Ms. Lars puts it. “Group efforts are always difficult. But in Saint-Henri, there’s a great community spirit. Maybe that’s why we’ve been successful; there’s a community that wants to make room for this.”
Avec Gaëlle Cerf et M’Lisa Colbert, Céci: Together with Gaëlle Cerf and M’Lisa Colbert, Cécile Lars oversees the management of the community fridge, from restocking to administrative tasks. The initiative requires more work than one might think: it takes a great deal of organization to collect donations, sort food and keep the place clean, all on a volunteer basis. By becoming a non-profit organization, the group behind the project hopes to be able to approach the City of Montréal and so establish new partnerships and get more donations. The three volunteers hope that once the project is well established, they will be able to approach all the merchants and restaurant owners in the neighbourhood to collect their unsold goods.
Pour le moment, seuls quelques-uns d’ent: For the moment, only a few of them have answered the call and donate to the fridge. “In the industry, there’s enormous waste. Maybe they don’t want to throw the products out, and we’re offering to come and pick them up,” Ms. Lars tells us.
Pour l’instant, les membres du frigo com: For now, the members of the community fridge don’t have access to a warehouse, another essential element. They used to have a space thanks to the generosity of a local organization, the Société de Développement Commercial (SDC) - Les Quartiers du Canal, which has since moved. The volunteers were able to store food received in large quantities and could cook it to offer baskets, which would have been greatly appreciated with the holidays approaching.
« C’est une activité qu’on a dû lâcher à: “It’s an activity we had to give up with great regret, it wasn’t manageable without a base of operations,” Ms. Lars explains. “In the meantime, we do the best we can with what we have, which has always been the mission of the fridge.”
L’idée d’un frigo communautaire a fait s: The idea of a community fridge has caught on <l1>in Montréal and elsewhere in Quebec</l1>. In the neighbouring area of Notre-Dame-de-Grâce, Seven Laville set up the Sunshine Food Pantry, where a fridge and a pantry are accessible 24 hours a day. “I created a Facebook page so people can follow it and see the updates. Anyone can comment and give,” explains Ms. Laville. After being turned down by the city, she turned to the generosity of a local business, Café 92, which agreed to host the fridge.
« Tout se passe bien. Nous avons eu des: “Everything’s going well. We’ve had ups and downs with people who take a lot,” she says. It’s a problem several people mentioned. There is a fine line between those who need a larger quantity of food for themselves or their loved ones and those who have other intentions than sharing.
Le garde-manger du Sunshine Food Pantry: The pantry of the Sunshine Food Pantry in Notre-Dame-de-Grâce, which also has a community fridge. Photo: Courtesy
Malgré tout, la jeune femme est heureuse: Despite everything, the young woman is happy to lead the project and praises the kindness of the neighbourhood residents who lend her a hand. “It’s the people who contribute. It’s what I like to do, I like to build, and it’s love to share,” she tells us. “I was a street kid, I was placed in foster care,” confides Ms. Laville, who says she once had to steal other children’s lunches at school.
Une fois adulte, elle a souhaité donner: As an adult, she wanted to give people the chance to eat by removing the obstacles to doing so. A few kilometres away, thanks to an initiative by students and children from Dawson College, a <l1>community pantry</l1> was set up last October on the grounds of the Congregation of Notre Dame.
John Nathaniel Gertler, l’un des instiga: John Nathaniel Gertler, one of the project’s instigators, sees it as an effort at mutual aid and relationship-building rather than a charitable initiative. “It’s the community that supports the project, not privileged people who are superior because they give to those who are less privileged,” he clarifies.
« On a été inspirés par plusieurs projet: “We were inspired by several mutual aid and community projects that appeared during the pandemic, both locally and internationally,” he explains, citing the fridges in Saint-Henri and Notre-Dame-de-Grâce, as well as the examples of Meals for Milton Park and Montreal Solidarity Supply. Mr. Gertler hopes a fridge can be added to the pantry, but this addition poses logistical challenges, on top of needing the approval of the hosts.
Le garde-manger du Atwater Community Pan: The pantry of the Atwater Community Pantry, at the Congregation of Notre Dame. Photo: Ruby Pratka
Depuis sa création, le garde-manger joui: Since its creation, the pantry has enjoyed enormous popularity, which speaks to the needs of the neighbourhood. In the immediate term, the volunteers want to increase the level of donations, and eventually be able to buy food. “We’d also like to be able to buy food and ask community members what they want to see in the pantry,” he says. The collective would like the support of more local businesses. Currently, two of them make donations. According to Mr. Gertler, several said they were giving elsewhere.
« Ils ont un système en place et disent: “They have a system in place and say they receive a large number of donation requests. People don’t understand how little we’re asking for. Our pantry is small, it would make a big difference. It illustrates a larger problem in the community sector in Montréal,” he believes. The student feels that several organizations have a monopoly on food distribution and that it’s difficult for a local project to claim its share, especially on the administrative side. In Montréal-Nord, a community fridge came into being in 2017 after the idea was proposed by residents. Unfortunately, the initiative ran out of steam and had to be discontinued, Olivier Lachapelle explains. The initiative was overseen by community organizations in the neighbourhood, Parole d’excluEs and Panier Fûté, which shared the premises where the fridge was located.
« Les tâches incombent souvent aux emplo: “The tasks often fall to employees, who don’t have the time and resources,” says Mr. Lachapelle. “The goal was for restaurant owners to take part, and that didn’t happen.” On top of the unpredictable nature of donations, mobilization was a problem. “I think if it had been carried by residents, it would have been a success,” he believes. In Villeray, the Frigo La Mie is the work of a dedicated resident, Johanne Bélanger.
Cinq ans plus tard, ce sont trois frigos: Five years later, three fridges and several shelves in her home are dedicated to people in the neighbourhood. Whenever food is available, Ms. Bélanger announces it in a Facebook group. People then make an appointment to pick up the items. “We need everything and nothing, that’s the problem,” she confides. She tells us the fridge is currently going through a “slow period” because she has received fewer food donations. When quantities allow, Ms. Bélanger also provides emergency food assistance, and other volunteers come to lend her a hand.
« Ce n’est pas seulement d’avoir un frig: “It’s not just about having a community fridge, at some point you get to know the stories of the people you meet,” she says. So she directs people to other resources, in addition to running another non-food donation project, <l1>DistribuDons.</l1> “Since I can’t work anymore, it fills my time. I like to help, and it’s nice to see people too,” says the woman, who lives with chronic pain. Despite her role as the neighbourhood’s fairy godmother, Ms. Bélanger is humble. “It’s easier to help than to ask,” she says. “It’s not thanks to me: if nobody gives me anything, I can’t help anybody. The people around are just as important. I’ll keep going as long as I have donations and as long as I’m able.”
